source.title: Homebrewed SLMs: Autoregressive and Masked Diffusion Language Models Built at Home for Portuguese

page_placements.theme: Tokenization, resolution and input allocation change effective scale

record.file_problem: The full paper text, including appendices, is present. There are minor equation and figure-text extraction artifacts, but they do not prevent reading the relevant results.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures held-out loss across repeated-training budgets and data amounts, and reports a substantial reversal in autoregressive loss at the longest budget. Its fixed-size, small-corpus experiments refine the scope of claims about loss scaling; they do not fit general scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The study does not vary parameter count or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation, and it does not fit power-law exponents or test small-run extrapolation. The legal-task results are reported at selected checkpoints rather than as downstream scaling curves, so they do not test V6. Cited scaling results from other papers are not recorded as rows. Training-partition loss and sample-quality results are not included as rows because the claim concerns held-out pretraining loss.
record.test_reason: A new setting: 11–12M-parameter Transformers trained on 0.6–1.1M-token Portuguese corpora, repeated for 1–256 epochs. Held-out bits per byte across compute budgets in this repeated-data regime bear on V5 (repeated data) and on the bending part of V7. The study fits no power law, sweeps no parameter count, and its epoch curves are data-bottlenecked, so they do not test V1. T5 does not fit: the authors make no argument against scaling laws; they report repetition curves for a tutorial.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. Correction: the authors find the autoregressive mode peaks at 64 epochs and then memorises, while diffusion keeps improving to 256 epochs; at their best points the two differ by less than the minimum effect. They call more text, with its compute, the clearest lever and recommend mixing with an n-gram. They caution that nothing transfers to larger scale without new measurement; they do not state that no broad scaling law is established.
record.recipe_differences: Unlike the original scaling-law studies, this work uses one small Transformer configuration per corpus and varies repeated-training budget and, in a separate curve, training-data amount. It does not sweep model size and tokens jointly, fit scaling exponents, or estimate compute-optimal allocations. The two generation modes use different objectives and attention masks.
record.method_sensitivity: Loss curves vary by generation mode, corpus, epoch budget, and training-data amount. Hyperparameters were selected at 256 epochs and held fixed across the budget grid. Equal-compute tokenizer controls also show large budget-dependent differences. A sensitivity analysis reports that the mode gap changes with window length, vocabulary size, and precision, without changing sign in its tested cases.

fits_no_version.finding: At equal compute, a byte-level tokenizer model is 0.8–1.4 bpb worse than BPE at the 16-epoch budget and about 1.0 bpb better at the 256-epoch budget. The authors attribute this to fewer passes over the data (r25–r28).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In data-constrained training, the tokenizer, through the number of passes it implies at fixed compute, can change held-out loss by more than the gains from extra compute.

fits_no_version.finding: Downstream legal task scores plotted against 6ND compute for the home model and for 160M/630M public models (Fig. 13). Public models lead on ordinary laws despite the home model's in-domain training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-model downstream comparison against training compute, uncontrolled for data and domain.

record.problems: The model scale is 11 to 12M parameters and the main corpus has about 0.62M training tokens; the authors explicitly state that nothing transfers to larger scale without new measurement. Only five repeated-training budgets are tested. The curves use fixed hyperparameters selected at the 256-epoch budget, and the autoregressive result at 256 epochs is conditional on the searched grid. The data-volume curve changes compute together with text amount. Diffusion results are NELBO bounds, whose gap to true likelihood is unmeasured. Bootstrap coverage failed for the decisive comparisons, which instead rely on six-seed randomization tests at their minimum attainable p-value.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible held-out loss results from the repeated-budget tables or external data curve were omitted. Training-partition losses, sample diagnostics, and legal-task outcomes were left out because they are not held-out pretraining-loss scaling measurements. The paper's cited external scaling results were not recorded as rows.

untested.parts: No parameter sweep. No compute or token curve with the other factors non-binding. The only unique-data curve spans 8x and is reported as gaps to a floor. No power-law fit.
No joint variation of N and D at fixed compute; no compute-optimal estimate.
One architecture (6 layers, d=384); no shape comparison at fixed N.
No other modalities, fine-tuning or transfer scaling. No power-law fit to the repeated-data curves. Single model size.
Legal tasks are scored only at best checkpoints. The Figure 13 compute comparison is across different public models with different data, not a controlled scale sweep.
No exponents fitted or compared. No parameter-counting, schedule or fitting-method comparison. No compute-optimal split.

missing.what: Absolute external-set bpb of the autoregressive model at each training-text fraction (needed to read a data-scaling trend; the text gives only gaps to a floor that is itself retrained)
AR validation bpb at 256 epochs across learning rate × dropout ranges from 2.850 to 5.818 (vs 1.851–2.023 at 16 epochs), showing the repeated-data reversal depends strongly on regularisation
At 256 epochs, AR loss across window (128/512) and vocabulary (2048/8192) varies from 2.650 to 2.994, vs diffusion 1.805–1.906

record.verdict_notes: The study is a tutorial, not a scaling-law study: one model size and five epoch budgets on tiny corpora. The reader's V1 'challenges' label is removed: repeated-epoch curves are data-bottlenecked, which V1 explicitly excludes. The V5 challenge is confined to extreme repetition (up to 256 epochs on 0.6M tokens) and is conditional on the regularisation grid. No original source is involved.

versions.untested_parts: Measures held-out loss across repeated epochs and a data-volume curve, but not loss across parameter counts, several orders of magnitude, or independently varied tokens and compute; no power law is fitted.
No small-run fit is used to predict much larger runs.
Parameter count and token count are not jointly varied at fixed compute; no compute-optimal allocation or scaling trend is estimated.
Depth, width, and other architecture details are not compared at fixed parameter count.
Tests repeated-text training in two language-modeling modes. Does not test other modalities, fine-tuning or transfer regimes generally, or whether a power-law form fits the repeated-data curves.
Legal task scores are not measured across a scale sweep or related systematically to pretraining loss.

Shows mode-, corpus-, budget-, and data-volume-dependent loss behavior, including a marked bend in autoregressive curves. Does not estimate or compare fitted exponents, test parameter-counting choices, or measure how fitting methods affect compute-optimal allocation.

relationships.reason: Held-out loss rises from 1.806 to 2.851 (A) and from 1.066 to 1.487 (B) as compute on repeated data grows, the opposite of a continuing fall (r4, r5, r14, r15). Training loss near 0.04 shows memorisation; the result depends on the regularisation grid.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Autoregressive mode, 1–64 epochs, corpora A and B
source_check.reason: Loss improves throughout this condition group. Diminishing returns are compatible with power-law improvement, and the study supplies no fit or explicit rejection of that form over 1–64 epochs. The later reversal belongs to l0; absence of a fitted form is untested evidence, not a scope limitation.

relationships.condition: Masked diffusion mode, 1–256 epochs, corpora A and B (NELBO bounds)
relationships.reason: The bound falls monotonically. On A it is nearly flat from 1 to 16 epochs (2.808→2.748), then drops steeply, a shape unlike a single power law in compute. No fit (r6–r10, r16–r20).
relationships.display_finding: Diffusion bounds decreased monotonically, but corpus A changed only from 2.808 to 2.748 over epochs 1–16 before dropping steeply, unlike a single power-law trend.

relationships.condition: Repeated-data epoch curves, both modes and corpora (bending part of V7 only)

relationships.display_finding: Autoregressive loss flattened and then rose after 64 epochs, whereas diffusion loss plateaued and then steepened, departing from a single compute power law.

labels.reason: Tables 4 and 6 show validation loss increasing from 1.806 to 2.851 and from 1.066 to 1.487. This contradicts continued power-law improvement in this repeated-data condition; the regularisation-grid restriction is explicit.

labels.label: limits_scope
labels.condition: Autoregressive mode, 1–64 epochs, corpora A and B
labels.reason: Loss improves throughout this condition group. Diminishing returns are compatible with power-law improvement, and the study supplies no fit or explicit rejection of that form over 1–64 epochs. The later reversal belongs to l0; absence of a fitted form is untested evidence, not a scope limitation.

labels.label: limits_scope
labels.condition: Masked diffusion mode, 1–256 epochs, corpora A and B (NELBO bounds)
labels.reason: Tables 4 and 6 show bound curves with an initial slow region followed by substantially faster improvement, qualifying a single power-law description of these reported bounds. This conclusion is restricted to NELBO bounds; their gap to true likelihood is unmeasured.

labels.label: supports
labels.condition: Repeated-data epoch curves, both modes and corpora (bending part of V7 only)
labels.reason: The autoregressive curves turn upward after 64 epochs, while the diffusion-bound curves change from slow to faster improvement. These support the bending component only; exponent and compute-optimal allocation dependence are untested.

relation.reason: Its held-out budget curves bear directly on repeated-data scaling and curve bending, despite the absence of fitted scaling laws.

tranche.reason: The study reports its own repeated-data budget curves in a new setting: small Portuguese language models on two corpora.

source_check.notes: All listed numerical values and conditions match Tables 4–6. Budget curves are descriptive except the 256-epoch cross-mode tests; hyperparameters are fixed across budgets after selection at 256 epochs, and diffusion measurements are upper bounds.

statements.correction: Table 5: byte-minus-BPE differences at the 16-epoch compute budget = +0.797 and +1.414 BPB; at the 256-epoch compute budget = −1.000 and −1.010 BPB. Byte-model passes at the latter budget = 81.3 and 71.8 versus BPE's 256. Fewer passes and less overfitting = proposed explanation, not separately tested; an intrinsic byte-modeling effect is not excluded.
statements.problem: The numerical summary is correct, but the explanation by differing passes is tentative rather than established.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Autoregressive mode on repeated text, corpora A and B, 64 to 256 epochs
reader_labels.reason: Held-out loss rises from 1.806 to 2.851 on corpus A and from 1.066 to 1.487 on corpus B, contrary to a continuing fall over this budget range (r4–r5, r14–r15). The study does not fit a power law.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Masked diffusion on repeated text, corpora A and B, 1 to 256 epochs
reader_labels.reason: The reported bound falls across the tested grid, but the study uses only one parameter scale per corpus and does not establish a power-law form or several-orders-of-magnitude range (r6–r10, r16–r20).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Autoregressive model with increasing corpus B training text
reader_labels.reason: External-set loss approaches the n-gram floor as data and compute increase together, but the last point is a tie and the study says the curve does not isolate training text from compute (r21–r24).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Autoregressive mode trained by repeated passes over the same text
reader_labels.reason: The held-out loss reverses between 64 and 256 epochs in both corpora, so this repeated-data regime does not show a continuing power-law fall across the full tested grid (r4–r5, r14–r15).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Masked diffusion mode trained by repeated passes over the same text
reader_labels.reason: The upper-bound loss improves across the grid, but no power law is fitted, and the result is specific to this small model and these two corpora (r6–r10, r16–r20).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Repeated-training budget curves across the two generation modes and corpora
reader_labels.reason: The curves depend strongly on training mode and corpus: autoregressive loss bends upward at 256 epochs while diffusion continues to improve through the end of the grid (r1–r20).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Equal-compute tokenizer controls on corpus A
reader_labels.reason: Changing from BPE to byte tokenization changes held-out loss substantially, and the direction depends on the budget, with the byte model worse at the 16-epoch-equivalent budget and better at the 256-epoch-equivalent budget (r25–r28).
